subject: electrical-computer
audience: FE Electrical and Computer candidates and engineering students
title: The /27 Network That Could Not Fit 40 Devices
featured_title: THE /27 NETWORK THAT COULD NOT FIT 40 DEVICES

presentation.challenge: The subnet looked large enough from the address range. The usable host count said otherwise.

practice.primary_question: Why can an IPv4 /27 subnet provide only 30 usable host addresses?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Counting all 32 addresses in a /27 block as usable host addresses and forgetting the network and broadcast addresses.

case_dna.target_misconception: A /27 subnet has 32 addresses, so it can support 32—or even 40—devices if addresses are assigned carefully.
case_dna.why_plausible: The block size is 32 addresses, and students may stop at the raw address count.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: A /27 leaves 5 host bits, giving 2^5=32 total addresses. In a conventional IPv4 subnet, one address is the network address and one is the broadcast address, leaving 30 usable hosts.
case_dna.corrected_model: For a conventional IPv4 subnet, total addresses are 2^(32-prefix), and usable host addresses are total minus 2.

problem_statement: A lab needs addresses for 40 IPv4 devices on one subnet. The proposed network is 192.168.10.0/27. The planner sees 32 addresses in the block and assumes the subnet is close enough. During deployment, addresses run out. Calculate the usable host capacity, identify the design error, and choose the smallest larger prefix that can support at least 40 hosts.
fixed_constraints: At least 40 usable host addresses required

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The /27 block existed. The host addresses ran out.
gates.prompt: How many of those 32 addresses are usable for ordinary hosts?
gates.cta: Separate total addresses from usable hosts

options.label: Usable hosts = 2^host_bits - 2 for a conventional IPv4 subnet
options.reason: The network and broadcast addresses are not assigned to ordinary hosts.

options.label: Usable hosts = all addresses in the block
options.reason: This counts the network and broadcast addresses as host addresses.

options.label: Usable hosts = the prefix length itself
options.reason: The prefix length tells how many bits identify the network, not the host count.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict usable host capacity
gates.prompt: A /27 has 5 host bits. How many usable host addresses are available?

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Allocate addresses across the subnet
gates.result: Only 30 addresses are available for ordinary hosts.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the host count
gates.hint: Reserve one address for the subnet ID and one for broadcast.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: The address block shows the missing capacity

cards.text: Five host bits create 32 total addresses.
After network and broadcast addresses are reserved, 30 ordinary host addresses remain.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the subnet plan
report: C3. Therefore it can support the required 40 host devices.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: Thirty-two total addresses cannot provide 40 usable host addresses.

evidence_choices.label: A /27 provides 30 usable hosts, while a /26 provides 62
evidence_choices.reason: This directly compares the capacity against the 40-host requirement.

correction.template: The /27 provides only {usable} usable host addresses, so it cannot support 40 devices.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Choose the smallest conventional subnet that fits 40 hosts
gates.constraint: Need at least 40 usable IPv4 host addresses.

options.label: Use a /26 subnet
options.reason: A /26 leaves 6 host bits: 64 total addresses and 62 usable hosts.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply the host-capacity rule
gates.prompt: How many usable hosts are available in a conventional IPv4 /28 subnet?

options.reason: A /28 leaves 4 host bits: 16 total minus network and broadcast = 14.
That counts network and broadcast as usable hosts.
The prefix length is not the host count.

gates.explanation: Usable hosts = 2^(32-prefix) - 2 for the conventional subnet cases used here.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the subnet calculation
gates.confirmation: I confirm that subnet design must distinguish total IPv4 addresses from usable host addresses.

items.label: What failed
items.value: The /27 subnet could not support 40 host devices.

items.label: What was assumed
items.value: All addresses in the block were treated as usable hosts.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Calculate total addresses from host bits, then subtract network and broadcast addresses for conventional IPv4 host capacity.

seo.seo_title: IPv4 /27 Subnet: Why It Has Only 30 Usable Hosts | FE E-038
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Case E-038: a /27 subnet has 32 total IPv4 addresses but only 30 usable hosts. Determine the smallest subnet for 40 devices.
seo.focus_keyphrase: IPv4 subnet host capacity FE exam
seo.excerpt: A /27 contains 32 addresses, but not all 32 can be assigned to ordinary hosts in a conventional IPv4 subnet.
seo.direct_answer: An IPv4 /27 prefix leaves 5 host bits, so the block contains 2^5=32 total addresses. Reserving the network and broadcast addresses leaves 30 usable host addresses. A /26 provides 62 usable hosts and can support 40 devices.

faqs.q: How many usable hosts are in a /27 subnet?
faqs.a: 30 usable hosts in a conventional IPv4 subnet.

faqs.q: What prefix can support at least 40 hosts?
